concept: Why do traffic jams appear out of nowhere?
title: Ghost Jam Circuit
tagline: A flawless loop with no bottleneck — yet traffic still snarls

science.hiddenLaw: On a uniform road with no bottleneck, phantom jams arise by string instability: above a critical vehicle density, finite driver reaction delay combined with safe-distance car-following causes any small braking perturbation to amplify upstream into a backward-propagating stop-and-go wave that lowers mean flow; below critical density or with zero delay the same perturbation decays and no jam forms.
science.plainStatement: Even with no crash or bottleneck, a tiny tap on the brakes can snowball into a traffic jam when cars are packed tightly: each driver behind brakes a little harder after a short reaction delay, creating a wave of stopped cars that travels backwards and reduces how many cars get through.
misconceptions: Traffic jams always require an external bottleneck such as an accident, lane closure, traffic light, or slow truck ahead.
Driving faster and following closer always increases road throughput (more cars per hour).
A traffic jam moves forward with the cars that created it, or stays fixed in place, rather than propagating backwards against traffic.
Phantom jams are caused by a few bad or inattentive drivers and would disappear if everyone drove skillfully, rather than being an emergent collective instability of dense flow itself.

sources.title: Sugiyama et al. (2008) Traffic jams without bottlenecks — experimental evidence for the physical mechanism of the formation of a jam, New Journal of Physics
Nagel & Schreckenberg (1992) A cellular automaton model for freeway traffic, J. Phys. I France
Treiber & Kesting - Traffic Flow Dynamics: Data, Models and Simulation (Springer) - Fundamental diagram and string instability
FHWA - Traffic Congestion Report: The Physics of Traffic Flow and Phantom Jams

story.setting: A pristine circular test track in the desert, filmed from above. No intersections, no accidents, no lane closures — just a perfect loop of asphalt and a fleet of identical test cars driving autonomously. You control the fleet size, the track length, how drivers react, and you can tap one car's brakes.
story.mystery: Engineers swear the road has no bottleneck, yet at certain times a cluster of stopped cars appears out of nowhere, crawls backwards against traffic, and chokes the flow. Other times the same tiny brake tap vanishes without a trace. The jam seems to have a life of its own.
story.goal: Find the hidden rule that decides when a whisper of braking becomes a ghost jam. Learn to predict when the wave will form, which way it moves, and why packing cars tighter can make fewer cars get through.

predictions.prompt: On this perfect loop with no accident, traffic light, or lane closure, you pack 30 cars onto a 300 m track, drivers react after 1.2 s, and you tap one brake by 2 m/s. What happens after 2 minutes?
options: A stop-and-go jam forms and persists even though there is no bottleneck
Nothing — without a bottleneck a jam cannot form, traffic just smooths out

predictions.prompt: The track is crowded (30 cars, 300 m, 1.2 s reaction). You raise the speed limit from 30 to 40 m/s while drivers keep the same 2 s preferred gap. What happens to throughput (cars per hour)?
options: Throughput falls as jams get worse — faster and closer does not always mean more flow
Throughput rises proportionally — faster and closer always means more cars per hour

predictions.prompt: A jam has formed on the loop. Which way does the jam itself move relative to the cars?
options: Backwards, upstream against traffic — the wave travels opposite to the cars
Forwards with the cars that created it, or stays fixed in place

predictions.prompt: You replace all drivers with identical, skillful drivers who all follow the same safe rule with 1.2 s reaction delay, keep the road crowded (30 cars, 300 m), and give one 2 m/s brake tap. What happens?
options: A jam still emerges — it is a collective instability of dense flow, not just a few bad drivers
No jam forms — with skillful drivers the tap smooths out and jams need bad drivers

transfer.setup: A circular warehouse conveyor belt carries packages with no narrow section or broken motor. Each robotic arm watches the package ahead and reacts after a short delay to keep a safe gap. One package is briefly held back by 2 units.
transfer.question: You increase package density from sparse (10 packages) to crowded (30 packages) while keeping the same reaction delay. What happens after the brief hold-back?
options: When sparse the wobble fades; when crowded it amplifies into a backward-moving jam of stopped packages that lowers throughput
The wobble always fades because there is no bottleneck
The jam moves forward with the packages
Adding more packages always raises throughput

checks.description: Above critical density with human reaction delay, a small perturbation amplifies into detectable stop-and-go jam(s)
Control: same reaction delay and perturbation but subcritical density - perturbations decay, no jam forms
Control: remove cause - zero reaction delay eliminates amplification even at supercritical density
Resulting jam wave propagates upstream opposite to traffic direction (negative wave speed)
Mean speed and flow decline over time as jam develops at supercritical density, disproving closer/faster always helps
